LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

Snake — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson handles the garden’s most serious card with a calm voice and a playful prop: scarf snakes to wiggle and coil, plus the honest rule delivered without drama or fear.

What is this?

A snake is a long animal with no legs that slithers smoothly over the ground. Garden snakes lie in sunny spots to warm up and mostly want to be left alone.

What does it mean?

The snake card is where the garden set gets serious, and toddlers can feel the shift. Handled calmly, it teaches the deepest safety lesson of all: some rules exist because the world has real edges.

What does the child need to know?

Snakes slither and like the sun. The rule comes in three moves: we never touch a snake, we step back slowly, and we tell a grown-up right away. Snakes are not nasty — they simply want their space, and we give it.

Why this matters

A two-year-old who can name the rule and the move owns it. Fear is not the goal — respect is. Calm repetition of a clear rule beats alarm, and the scarf game keeps the snake friendly in imagination while the rule stays real.

What it teaches

Rule-learning with three clear steps, calm body response (step back, not scream), long-and-short vocabulary, scarf play for arm strength and coordination, and trust that grown-ups handle the scary bits.

Words to learn

snakeslithersunlongbacktell

Say this to your child

“"A snake — sssss. It is long and it slithers on its belly, with no legs at all. Here is our snake rule, and it is an important one: we never touch snakes. If we ever see one, we step back slowly and we tell me. A snake’s whole wish is to be left in peace — and peace is what we give it."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card, say snake, and make a long sssss — long and slow, the sound the animal makes in every storybook.
  2. Draw the shape with your arm: a snake is one long curve with no legs — let your toddler trace it in the air with a finger.
  3. Grab a long scarf — your stand-in snake — and wriggle it over the floor together, then coil it in a warm circle for its nap.
  4. Say the rule in three beats, keeping your voice level and kind: see a snake — step back slowly — tell a grown-up. Practise the three beats like a little song.
  5. Close with calm: snakes live in the garden too, and they are happiest when we give them room — the scarf snake can live in the toy box, the real one stays outside.

Look closer at the picture

Say snake and stretch one arm into a long, slow curve — no legs anywhere. Make the sssss sound softly, ask what the snake is doing in the sun, and trace its long shape on the rug with one finger.

Ask your child

"What does the snake say?" "How many legs does a snake have?" "What do we do if we see a real snake?" "Who do we tell?" — the last two answered with the practised chant: step back, tell you.

What your child can say or do

"Sssss!" "Step back, tell Mummy!" Expect scarf snakes everywhere, snakes audited in every picture book, and the rule recited with solemn pride. Calm respect — not fear — is the sound of this lesson working.

Out in the real world

Garden snakes sun themselves on warm paths, walls and woodpiles in many places. Every real sighting — rare and brief — is the rule performed exactly as rehearsed: back slowly, find the grown-up.

Try it together

Scarf snake trail: lay the scarf in wiggles along the floor and walk the line heel-to-toe like a tightrope, then coil it in a basket for its nap. Wiggles out, rule intact, snake tucked in.

Understanding check

Ask casually what we do if we find a snake outside: the three-beat answer — back slowly, tell a grown-up, never touch — means the most important rule in the set is home.

Parent tips

Keep your voice flat and warm when the rule comes up; drama teaches fear where calm teaches competence. Retell the rule in new places — parks, holidays, grandma’s garden — so it travels like the scarf does.

Staying safe

This is the set’s real-deal safety card: never touch, reach for or corner any snake, and treat every unknown snake as a keep-away snake. If one appears often near your home, mention it to local wildlife services — not to your toddler.

This lesson pairs with the Snake flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).
